mustInclude: An account of the visit and of the beginners' session itself (who went or when, what the instructor did, what the climbing was like), consistent with the advertisement (90 minutes, small group, safety talk, auto-belay walls / bouldering area)

A rating for each of the four areas in the form (Staff, Safety, Price, Facilities) with a reason for each rating, using details from the advertisement or the visit rather than copying the advertisement
A recommendation saying what kind of person the gym suits (e.g. complete beginners, groups of friends, people afraid of heights)
genreFeatures: Online review: a reviewer's first-person voice, an overall opinion that is clear early on, and evaluative language (worth it, let down by, the highlight was)
Ratings may be shown as stars or numbers next to each area, or worked into the text; either is acceptable as long as each rating is explained
A review title (the form has a box for one) and the writer's name are credited if present but not required by the content points
About 200 words: one short paragraph per main idea
taskRequirements.registerTone: Informal and lively, written for other young people on a review website: personal and honest, with some humour or enthusiasm, but clear enough to help a reader decide. Not essay-like (no 'In conclusion') and not a formal complaint.
pitfalls: Copying the advertisement's lists (opening hours, all facilities) instead of evaluating them
Giving star ratings with no reasons, or explaining only one or two of the four areas
Recommending the gym to 'everyone' instead of saying who it suits
Forgetting the improvement suggestion, or making a suggestion unrelated to the visit
Contradicting the advertisement (e.g. a 3-hour session, paying the student price without being a student, a large group of 20)
Writing an essay on the benefits of sport rather than a review of this gym
Essay connectives and formal endings (Firstly, In conclusion) that do not suit a website review

content.high: All three points are covered with specific, consistent details; each of the four ratings is justified by something that happened during the visit or a fair judgement of the advertised facts (e.g. weighing the student price against what is included); the recommendation names a clear type of visitor and the improvement follows from a weakness mentioned earlier; a reader could decide whether to go.
content.mid: All three points are attempted, but some ratings are explained only briefly or generally, the recommendation is vague (e.g. 'people who want to try something new'), or some details are lifted from the advertisement without comment.
content.low: Only part of the task is done: ratings are given without reasons, the session itself is barely described, the improvement or recommendation is missing, and large parts are copied from the advertisement or drift into general comments about sport.

language.high: Accurate and varied sentences with a natural, conversational review voice; precise evaluative vocabulary (gently, out of place, packed); past tenses for the visit and present tenses for judgements are handled correctly.
language.mid: Simple sentences mostly accurate; errors in tense, agreement and prepositions (listen the talk, the facilities is) and some Chinese-influenced structures, but meaning is clear; vocabulary adequate but plain (very good, very convenient).
language.low: Frequent errors in basic grammar (I go last week, it is very safety) that sometimes obscure meaning; vocabulary limited and often taken from the advertisement; tone uneven.

organisation.high: Opens with an engaging hook or overall verdict, moves logically through the session, the four ratings and the recommendation; paragraphs are short and focused; linking is smooth and suits a review.
organisation.mid: Paragraphs follow the content points in order, but linking is mechanical (First, About safety, In conclusion) and the ending is a formula rather than a verdict.
organisation.low: Ideas are listed in loosely defined paragraphs with little linking; the order follows the advertisement rather than the reviewer's experience; the ending is abrupt or a general slogan.

1.notes: Any reasonable date of visit, companions, instructor name and star ratings are accepted as long as they do not contradict the advertisement and each rating is explained. A candidate may pay the full price or the student price; if the student price is mentioned it should be $180. A title is not required but is credited as good awareness of the form. Over-length reviews earn nothing extra. Candidates need not reproduce the form's name/date boxes; a semi-formal but friendly tone is also acceptable. Several improvement suggestions are not penalised if at least one is specific.

mustInclude: Reasons why many young adults in Hong Kong live with their parents for longer (e.g. housing costs and rents, waiting time for public housing, longer study, unstable or low-paid first jobs, family expectations or caring for parents), explained rather than merely listed
A clear position on whether living with parents after starting work is a smart choice, kept consistent throughout (yes, no, or yes/no with conditions)
Arguments with explanation or examples supporting that position
genreFeatures: Essay for a magazine competition: a title is expected; introduction with a clear thesis, body paragraphs each developing one main reason or argument, and a conclusion that returns to the question
Third person or general first person; personal examples (a cousin, a neighbour) may be used as evidence
taskRequirements.registerTone: Formal to semi-formal and reasoned, written to persuade competition judges and magazine readers. Confident but not preachy; avoids lecturing young people or blaming them.
pitfalls: Explaining the reasons only and never answering 'a smart choice?'
Writing 'advantages and disadvantages' with no final position, when the question asks the writer to argue either that it is or that it is not a smart choice
Treating the topic as being about teenagers or students who obviously live at home, rather than young adults in their twenties
Writing about teenagers growing up slowly or becoming mature in general, rather than the decision to live with parents after starting work
Drifting into complaints about strict parents or into housing policy demands unrelated to the question
Listing reasons in single sentences with no explanation (Firstly … Secondly … Thirdly)
Stating figures as fact without hedging; invented statistics are acceptable only as support, not as the whole argument

content.high: Two or three reasons are explained with Hong Kong-relevant detail, and the stance is argued with developed points (savings, family support, time to plan a career) and a counter-argument that is answered convincingly; the writer may set conditions (pay your way, set a date), showing mature thinking; ideas are tailored to young readers of a youth magazine.
content.mid: Reasons and a stance are both present, but development is uneven: some points are listed rather than explained, examples are thin or partly irrelevant, and the counter-argument is mentioned but dismissed in one line.
content.low: Reasons are mentioned briefly or repeated; no clear stance (advantages and disadvantages only) or a stance that changes; irrelevant personal material (e.g. about the writer's own strict parents); parts misunderstand who 'young adults' are.

language.high: Wide range of accurate structures (concession, conditionals, contrast) and precise vocabulary on housing and family life used naturally; formal but readable; very few slips.
language.mid: Generally accurate simple sentences; complex sentences contain errors (the reason is the price of flats is high; will become not independent); some word-form and agreement errors; vocabulary adequate but repetitive.
language.low: Frequent errors in agreement, word form and sentence structure (live with parents have good and bad; it is depend on) that often affect meaning; very limited vocabulary, much of it from the question.

organisation.high: Clear thesis, logically ordered paragraphs moving from causes to evaluation to rebuttal, and a conclusion that adds a final insight; cohesion is varied and subtle.
organisation.mid: Clear paragraphs with topic sentences but mechanical linking (First of all, Moreover, Furthermore); conclusion largely repeats the introduction.
organisation.low: Some paragraphing, but ideas jump between causes, opinions and personal remarks; little linking; the conclusion introduces a new idea or contradicts the body.

2.notes: Either stance (a smart choice / not a smart choice) or a conditional stance is equally acceptable if argued consistently. Personal examples and candidate-invented figures may be used to support points; marks depend on the reasoning, not on whether figures are accurate. A response that only explains the reasons cannot score above 4 in Content. Addressing the opposite view is credited at the higher bands but is not required.

mustInclude: A clear statement that the writer is applying for the summer guide job
Relevant experience or qualities for leading groups of primary school children, supported by evidence
Interest in the gallery's subject (toys and games from Hong Kong's past) and why the writer wants this job
genreFeatures: Formal letter layout: salutation 'Dear Ms Fong', paragraphs, closing 'Yours sincerely' and the name Chris Wong
Opening paragraph states the purpose; body paragraphs each focus on one area of suitability; final paragraph refers to next steps
taskRequirements.registerTone: Formal, confident and polite: a young applicant writing to an adult employer. Shows enthusiasm through specific evidence rather than repeated claims (I am hard-working, I am responsible); no pleading or demands.
pitfalls: 'Dear Sir/Madam' or 'Dear Sir' although Ms Fong is named; 'Yours faithfully', 'Best wishes' or signing with a first name only
Listing adjectives about oneself with no evidence
Ignoring the gallery's subject, or treating the job as babysitting rather than guiding and explaining
Writing mainly about why museums are important in general
Demanding a quick reply or asking about pay first
Inventing an age outside 16–19

content.high: All areas are covered with concrete, credible evidence (what the writer did with children and what they learnt from it); a genuine link to old toys and games is shown, perhaps with an idea for engaging young visitors; the letter as a whole would convince an employer.
content.mid: The main areas are covered, but evidence is general or only partly relevant to guiding children; interest in the gallery is stated with little development; self-praise replaces some evidence.
content.low: A short, thin application: only general claims (I like children, I like museums); misunderstands the job as looking after children; little or no link to the gallery.

language.high: Accurate, varied sentences with an assured formal tone; precise vocabulary for skills and experience; register is consistent from salutation to sign-off.
language.mid: Mostly accurate simple sentences; errors with prepositions, word forms and verb patterns (apply the job, interesting in, experience to work); some lapses in register.
language.low: Frequent basic errors (take care her, I never late, many museum) and comma splices that sometimes affect meaning; register swings between informal and pleading.

organisation.high: Purpose stated at once; each paragraph develops one area of suitability; smooth transitions; correct formal layout throughout.
organisation.mid: Clear paragraphing but mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly, Also); layout mostly correct with a mismatched sign-off.
organisation.low: Short, loosely connected paragraphs; incorrect layout (Dear Sir, Best wishes, first name only); ideas listed without development.

3.notes: Any school name (fictional), experience and availability are acceptable; if an age is given it should be 16–19. Age (16–19), how the post was found, availability and an offer to attend an interview are credited but not required; mentioning an enclosed CV or referee is likewise credited but not required. Candidates do not need to know real museum details; reasonable ideas for guiding children are credited.

mustInclude: The purpose of the report and how the information was gathered (survey and two weeks of observation)
Findings on how students use the library after school, e.g. who comes, at what times, what they do there, and any problems observed
Recommendations that follow from the findings
genreFeatures: Report layout: To / From / Date / Subject lines or a clear report title, and headings such as Introduction, Method, Findings, Recommendations, Conclusion
Findings presented objectively, ideally with figures or proportions from the survey or observation (candidate-invented data accepted)
Recommendations may be numbered; about 400 words
taskRequirements.registerTone: Formal and objective: a student reporting to the Student Council. Findings are stated neutrally rather than as personal complaints; recommendations are practical and politely worded.
pitfalls: Writing a letter or an essay of personal opinion instead of a report with headings
Giving opinions about the library ('I like to go there every day') instead of findings
No reference to the survey or observation; findings with no figures or examples
Recommendations unrelated to the findings or unrealistic (open until midnight)
Only describing problems and giving no recommendations

content.high: Method is clear; findings are specific and backed by figures or observed examples covering both use and problems; recommendations are practical, numbered and clearly linked to particular findings; the Student Council could act on the report.
content.mid: Purpose, findings and recommendations are all present, but findings are general (most students, some students) with little data, and recommendations are partly general (make more rules, hold reading activities).
content.low: Reads as a personal opinion piece or letter; findings are mixed with the writer's own experiences and complaints; few or unrealistic recommendations; the survey is barely used.

language.high: Accurate, concise and objective; a range of structures for reporting results (fewer than, made up nearly, were seen waiting); precise vocabulary; no slips in register.
language.mid: Simple reporting sentences mostly accurate; errors in tense (the library opens since), articles, word form (better than study at home) and some Chinese-influenced structures (This make other students cannot concentrate).
language.low: Frequent errors in tense, agreement and plurals (many student go, the librarian don't) that sometimes obscure meaning; informal, personal tone.

organisation.high: Full report layout with logical headings and numbered points; each recommendation clearly matches a finding; concise conclusion.
organisation.mid: Headings are used but the To/From/Subject block is missing or incomplete; findings and recommendations are paragraphed but linking is mechanical (Moreover, Firstly).
organisation.low: Letter or essay format with no headings; ideas move between findings, opinions and suggestions with little order.

4.notes: Candidates must invent their survey results; any reasonable numbers are accepted and should not be treated as fact. The library's 6.30 pm closing time is given; recommendations to change it are acceptable if justified by findings. Recommendations may target how the library is used or the opening hours, but must follow from the findings; a report that becomes an argument about whether to keep late opening loses Content.

mustInclude: The bet and the writer accepting it (details are the candidate's choice)
How the weekend went: specific moments, temptations or difficulties and how the writer dealt with them
How the weekend ended (whether the writer managed it)
What the writer learnt from the experience
genreFeatures: Personal blog post: a catchy title, first-person narrative voice, direct address to readers, and a natural ending (e.g. a question to readers or a comment invitation)
Mainly narrative in past tenses, with reflection in present tenses; sub-headings are optional
taskRequirements.registerTone: Informal, personal and engaging, for readers of the writer's own blog; humour and honesty are welcome. Reflection should sound personal rather than like a lecture to readers.
pitfalls: Writing an essay on 'how teenagers can save money' with little or no story
Narrating the weekend as a timetable (I woke up, I ate, I slept) without any tension or memorable moments
Ending with a moral lecture (Everyone should save money) instead of a personal reflection
Forgetting to say whether the bet was won
Breaking the challenge without noticing (e.g. paying for transport or snacks)
Treating it as a 'challenge website' post or discussing whether to continue the challenge forever (not required)

content.high: A vivid, well-chosen story: the bet is set up clearly, there are concrete temptations (friends buying drinks, transport costs) and inventive solutions, the result is given, and the reflection is personal and insightful (spending as habit, what really matters); strong sense of a blog audience.
content.mid: The weekend is narrated with some relevant moments and the result is given, but events are told in sequence with limited detail, and the reflection turns into general lessons (Firstly, money is not the most important thing).
content.low: Little narrative: mostly general comments or advice about saving money; the experience is thin or confusing; the reflection is a slogan.

language.high: Natural, varied sentences with a convincing conversational voice; accurate narrative tenses (past perfect where needed); vivid word choice without forced idioms.
language.mid: Simple narrative sentences mostly accurate, but frequent tense shifts between past and present and some agreement errors; vocabulary plain (very sad, very boring).
language.low: Frequent errors in tense, agreement and plurals (my friend say, I not buy anything, many way) that often affect meaning; very limited vocabulary.

organisation.high: Engaging opening, clear progression through the weekend (perhaps with sub-headings), a satisfying ending that links back to the bet; cohesion is smooth.
organisation.mid: Chronological paragraphs that are easy to follow, but a formulaic ending (Firstly … Secondly … Thirdly) and some abrupt transitions.
organisation.low: Essay-style introduction and conclusion around a short, under-developed story; paragraphs are loosely connected.

5.notes: The amount of the bet, the setting and the outcome (won or lost) are the candidate's choice; a writer who loses the bet but reflects well can score highly. Meals provided at home are not a breach of the challenge unless the candidate's own rules say so. Grey areas (a pre-loaded transport card, parents paying, food already at home) are for the candidate to decide and may be part of the story; a stake need not be named.
